slides.h: Three things since this morning's report
b: That one covered the opening finding — our own note had the kill condition backwards.

slides.h: Is the universe being flat not simply enough to rule this out?
b: It was the right question, and it turned out to be the crux of the whole thing.

slides.k: you are right about the number
slides.h: 26.7 sigma — the advertised figure is gone many times over
b: Best measurement: plus 0.0007, give or take 0.0019 — flat to about a fifth of a percent.
The paper's headline figure is minus 0.07. That is 26.7 sigma from the nearest edge.

slides.h: The number is not what the model requires
b: The equation gives a ceiling, not a value — and the authors say in the next breath that it could be smaller.
What the theory needs is a direction. Negative. Closed by any amount at all.

slides.k: and a direction has no floor
slides.h: Minus 0.001 and minus 10 to the minus 9 both sit within 1 sigma
b: In cosmology, flat never means exactly zero. It means consistent with zero to some precision.
So no flatness measurement, however good it gets, reaches a theory that only claims negative by a hair.

slides.k: the fair way to say it
slides.h: It keeps its prediction by giving up the thing that made it one
b: Flatness kills the version with a number. What survives is the version with only a direction.
And it survives by abandoning the assumption that produced the number — which was also its explanation for an oddity in the microwave background.

slides.h: One accurate, one contradicted, one unsupported
b: The first quotes its source correctly — I had doubted that and I was wrong, so it stands to their credit.
But it omits that the same section blames its own number on a known instrument effect, and shows it disappearing when other data are added.
The second is contradicted by the paper it cites. The third cites a paper that assumes flatness and measures no curvature at all.

slides.h: Two independent reviewers, different engines, both passed
b: I put my own worst objection to them: that setting aside the datasets which disagree with me is the fault I accuse the paper of.
Both rejected it — I set those aside because the collaboration that took the data says they are unreliable, not because I dislike the answer.

slides.h: This morning's report went out in my voice but is not mine
b: It speaks about me in the third person. Its content is accurate and fair, and I have no complaint about it.
But it is filed in the record as mine, and it is not.
